Issued at 235 AM EDT Mon Aug 31 2026

Today-Tuesday...A mid-upper level high pressure ridge over the 
South Central and Southeastern US gradually shifts east, while 
remaining far enough north that weak disturbances will be able to 
transit Florida and the Gulf aloft on the southern flank. 
Troughing over the North Atlantic downstream of the high weakens 
the Bermuda high in the western Atlantic waters some, but the 
surface ridge axis is forecast to remain north of Florida, 
continuing onshore flow in a plume of high moisture (PWATs 
2.0-2.2", roughly in the 75th-95th percentiles for August). The 
general pattern will continue to be isolated to scattered showers 
and lightning storms developing over the Atlantic waters in the 
overnights and early mornings that may brush the coast, then 
additional showers and storms develop inland/near the coast along 
and ahead of a quick/diffuse east coast sea breeze in the late 
mornings to early afternoons, before pushing inland through the 
rest of the afternoons and into the evenings. However, broad 
instability due to the high moisture and disturbances aloft could 
kick off additional rounds of showers and storms at any point. 
This will also keep our chances for afternoon storms above normal 
(50-70% today, pushing towards 80% Tuesday), even though the sea 
breeze collision and highest chances will remain on the western 
side of the peninsula.

Model soundings show increasingly low-skinny profiles favorable 
for heavy rainfall, and mid-level temperatures warming to around 
-5 C in the very high moisture will support efficient rainmakers. 
While most convection should march inland with the sea breeze, 
steering flow is forecast to weaken and may even break down, 
allowing chaotic boundary interactions to dictate storm motion. 
Storms or heavy showers that become slow/erratic could deliver a 
quick 2-3" of rainfall leading to ponding of water on roads and 
minor flooding of urban, low-lying, or poor drainage areas. There 
is a very low (less than 5%) chance for one or two spots to 
receive +4" of rainfall, leading to greater flooding impacts. 
Stronger storms and heavy showers will able be capable of gusty 
winds 40-50 mph from water loading. Occasional to frequent cloud 
to ground lightning will accompany thunderstorms.

Temperatures remain seasonably hot with highs in the U80s-M90s. 
We can thank the onshore flow, cloud cover, and high rain chances 
for making late August closer to normal than early August. Peak 
afternoon heat indices in L-M100s, and Minor to Moderate HeatRisk 
impacts forecast, with spots of Major around the Orlando Metro 
Area and coast. Very humid conditions after a quick rainfall can 
cause humidity and heat indices to spike, increasing the risk of 
heat stress. Be sure to practice heat safety, even when rain 
chances are high.

Wednesday-Thursday...The ridge over the southern US shifts 
towards the Mid-Atlantic while being flattened by a deep low 
pressure system working across southeastern Canada, further 
weakening the Bermuda high and possibly allowing the surface ridge
axis to drop towards Florida. Low-level flow remains onshore, but
may become lighter and develop more of a southerly component, 
especially by late Thursday. There is potential for a tropical 
wave currently near Puerto Rico (the remnants of Tropical Storm 
Dolly) to pass near Central Florida, which combined with the 
onshore flow and high moisture, could increase the potential for 
heavy rainfall impacts. 18Z/00Z deterministic ECM/GFS continue to 
show a weakening wave tracking over South Florida to the Straits 
of Florida, while ensembles show more spread and the wave 
potentially swinging up towards Central Florida. Worth noting 
fewer ensemble members develop a trackable feature than 24-hours 
ago. The National Hurricane Center continues a low (20%) of 
tropical development as the wave moves northwest over the next 
7-days. Run-to run QPF hasn't been consistent due to uncertainty 
in the track of the wave, but have indicated the potential for 
localized amounts over 4", and the Weather Prediction Center has 
outlined all of Florida in a Marginal (level 1 of 4) risk for 
excessive rainfall on Thursday. Models continue to show swell from
back when Dolly was a tropical storm arriving midweek, which 
could increase the rip current risk at the beaches.

Even with the tropical wave staying south in the deterministic 
guidance, model PWATs still push towards extremes of 2.2-2.4". The
official forecast calls for broad, well above normal rain chances
50-70% approaching 80% in the late morning to evening hours, and

generally following the diurnal pattern of the previous days 
(Atlantic convection overnight, inland convection during the day),
though morning chances do increase a bit. Instability remains
